_doc: College and junior college scenarios. Field reference: the _doc in scenarios_hs.json.

scenarios.title: Heavy Class Load
scenarios.text: Midterms in three classes the same week, and your position coach wants extra film sessions.

choices.label: Prioritize football
choices.result: Your grades slip a little. Your kicking doesn't.

choices.label: Get a tutor and balance it
choices.result: Organized and on top of it.

scenarios.title: Roommate Trouble
scenarios.text: Your roommate games with friends until 3 a.m. every night.

choices.label: Crash on a teammate's couch
choices.result: Fun, but your back hates you.

scenarios.title: Endorsement Offer
scenarios.text: Gridiron Grub, a local burger spot, wants you in a TV spot for a few hundred dollars.

choices.label: Sign and film it
choices.result: You're on TV. Your teammates won't let it go.

choices.label: Negotiate with the athletic department's help
Pass and focus on the season

scenarios.title: The Ad Drops
scenarios.text: Your Gridiron Grub commercial is running during every local broadcast.

choices.label: Laugh it off and stay humble

scenarios.title: Team Tradition
scenarios.text: Upperclassmen tell the rookies to skip study hall and do a midnight 'team tradition' run around campus.

choices.label: Go along with it
choices.result: It's harmless, but you're exhausted and behind on school.

choices.label: Politely decline
choices.result: A few guys call you soft. Your grades thank you.

choices.label: Talk to the captain about it
choices.result: He makes it optional. Some rookies are grateful.

scenarios.title: Homesick
scenarios.text: First time this far from home. The dorm feels very quiet.

choices.label: Keep it to yourself
choices.result: It sits with you all week.

scenarios.title: Finals Crunch
scenarios.text: Two finals and a paper due the week of a big conference game.

scenarios.title: Media Day
scenarios.text: Cameras everywhere. Reporters want five minutes with the kicker.

choices.label: Keep it short
choices.result: You're back on the practice field in no time.

choices.label: Own the room
choices.result: The cameras love you. You walk out buzzing.

scenarios.title: New Coordinator, New Technique
scenarios.text: The new special teams coordinator wants to rebuild your approach angle.

choices.label: Keep your own style
choices.result: He's not thrilled, but your kicks are good.

scenarios.title: Internship or Training?
scenarios.text: A summer internship at a sports analytics firm, or a summer of full-time training?

choices.label: Take the internship
choices.result: You learn a ton. Your leg gets a little rusty.

scenarios.title: Scouts at Practice
scenarios.text: Pro scouts are timing your hang time at practice this week.

choices.label: Boom every kickoff
choices.result: Hang times the scouts can't ignore.

choices.label: Talk shop with the scouts after

scenarios.title: Earn Your Spot
scenarios.text: As a walk-on, you're third on the depth chart. Coach says the job goes to whoever earns it in camp.

choices.label: Outkick the scholarship guy
choices.result: You win the job on the last day of camp.

choices.label: Learn everything from the starter
choices.result: He's impressed by how fast you learn.

choices.label: Ask coach exactly what he needs

scenarios.title: Combine Invite
scenarios.text: You've been invited to the pro scouting combine after the season.

choices.label: Train for the testing
choices.result: Your leg has never been stronger.

choices.label: Prepare for team interviews
choices.result: You'll walk in ready for every question.

scenarios.title: Academic Probation Warning
scenarios.text: The academic office warns you: below a 2.0 GPA you can't play.

choices.label: Hope for the best
choices.result: Hope is not a study plan.

authoring.premise: {parent} helps you carry boxes into a cinderblock dorm room and lingers at the door longer than either of you expected.
{coach} lays out the rules on day one: curfew, study hall, phones in the bin at meetings, and one strike before the coach calls home.
Three weeks in, the dining hall, the dorm and the practice field all feel like someone else's life, and nobody here knew you before.
Your high school group chat goes quiet. {best_friend} posts photos from a new school with new friends, and you realize you haven't texted anyone in a week.
Your assigned roommate games until four in the morning, and your first lift is at six.
Your academic advisor, {teacher}, sets your schedule: six hours of study hall a week, signed in and out, or you lose eligibility.
The senior kicker you're replacing next year can make your life easy or miserable, and he hasn't decided which.
You're paying your own way while scholarship players get meal cards and gear you don't. A teammate jokes that walk-ons are practice dummies.
A freshman kicker who's redshirting this year sits out every game and watches you kick. He's lonely, bitter, and good.
Upperclassmen throw the first big party of the year on a Thursday. The 6 a.m. lift is in seven hours, and everyone is watching what the freshmen do.
The seniors announce freshman duties: carry their bags, sing the fight song at dinner, fetch whatever they ask for.
The freshman 'initiation' night arrives, and it's not singing anymore. Some of what the seniors have planned is humiliating, and some of it could hurt someone.
{love_interest} is back home, the calls are getting shorter, and you keep missing each other between practice and class.
The team practices straight through the holiday. {sibling} calls to ask why you're not coming home this year.
Your first road game: a hotel, a curfew check at eleven, and two upperclassmen planning to sneak out to a party across town.
Your aid paperwork comes with a line you skipped: a minimum GPA to keep it. Midterms are in three weeks.
You owned your first mistake, and the staff believed you. Now there's another one, and {coach} wants to know whether the first apology meant anything.
authoring.note: Opens only on a strike after owning the first one (The Coach's Office clears strikes). The good choice sets owned_it_again and second_chance_used; the bad one sets character_concerns.

authoring.premise: The athletic department offers every player sessions with a sports psychologist. Most of the team jokes about it.
Alumni pack the campus for homecoming. Boosters want photos, the band wants the specialists for a skit, and the team wants you rested.
A friendly booster shakes your hand after practice and leaves something in it: a prepaid card 'for a nice dinner.'
A local sandwich shop offers a small deal: free food all season and a few posts. It's legal, but it's your name on it.
It's the middle of the semester and your account is nearly empty. Rent, books and a phone bill are due the same week.
{tyler} is a college kicker now too, and your names keep showing up next to each other on the same lists.
Your new holder, {holder}, spins the laces a different way than you're used to, and neither of you wants to be the one to change.
You haven't slept more than four hours before a game all season. You lie awake replaying kicks you haven't attempted yet.
A D on your chemistry midterm. Your advisor will see it Friday whether you tell them or not.
A teammate in your class wants his name on your group project. He hasn't come to a single meeting.
The senior captain pulls you aside: some of the guys think you act like you're too good for the team.
A trick-shot clip of you from practice goes around campus, and suddenly people you don't know want a picture.
A fan account tears into you after a loss. Your thumb is already on the reply button.
{parent} sounds tired on the phone. His hours got cut, he says, but it's nothing for you to worry about.
{sibling} comes to campus for a weekend and wants to see everything: the locker room, the dorm, the parties he's heard about.
An upperclassman offers you a folder of last year's exams for your hardest class. 'Everybody uses them,' he says.
Winter workouts start at 5:30 a.m. in the dark. Three teammates have already started skipping and signing each other in.
Spring practice opens with a kicking competition for next season. The veteran kicker is graduating, and the job is wide open.
{coach} closes the door. Word of what you did got back to the staff, and the coach wants to hear it from you before deciding anything.
Your tutor offers to 'clean up' your history paper. You both know that means writing it.
Your hip is sore, and a teammate offers you some of his prescription. 'It's basically nothing,' he says.
An off-campus party gets out of hand fast. Campus security is on the way, and a teammate who's in bad shape can't find his ride.
The athletic department opens an investigation into last year's initiation night, and investigators want to talk to every sophomore.
The new freshmen arrive, and the seniors look at your class. Freshman duties are yours to run now, or to end.
{coach} signs a scholarship freshman kicker, {backup}, and assigns them to share your reps and your locker row.
Fall camp turns into a public competition with {backup}. Every kick is charted, and the depth chart comes out Friday.
{coach} rewatches your old recruiting tape and stops on one clip. 'Tell me about this one,' the coach says.
Friends at other schools look happier, and a teammate keeps talking about the transfer portal like it's an escape hatch.
A coach from another school calls you directly, which isn't allowed. He says there's a spot for you if you ever 'get curious.'
Your practice charts are the worst they've been since high school, and you can't stop thinking about it, even in class.
Before warmups your chest goes tight, your hands won't stop shaking and you can't get a full breath.
A groin strain flares on every kickoff. The trainer wants you out a week; the season says otherwise.
A guy at the gym swears by a powder that isn't on the team's approved list. Two teammates already use it.
You go home for the first time in months. Your old room is a storage closet now, and everyone talks about people you don't know.
A classmate from your statistics class asks if you want to study together, and it doesn't feel like it's only about studying.
{best_friend} calls at midnight: they're failing out of school and haven't told their family.
{parent} finally tells you: the cut hours became a layoff. He says he'll figure it out.
The school's NIL collective offers a monthly deal for appearances at booster events. It's real money, and it's a lot of evenings.
A car dealer who sits behind the bench offers you a 'loaner' for the semester. No paperwork, he says.
The team picks you to speak at conference media day, live, with a dozen microphones in your face.
Rivalry week: someone painted your statue overnight, and teammates plan a midnight trip to the other campus to return the favor.
A kicker from your school who made it to the pros offers to train you for a week this summer, at his own cost.
Summer is three choices: summer classes to get ahead, a kicking camp circuit, or a job back home.
{holder} wants to stop holding to focus on winning a starting job elsewhere on the roster.
{teacher} calls you in: one more bad grade and you're academically ineligible.
Your apartment is the obvious place for the team party, and everyone's already planning it.
Your roommate's late nights have turned into parties in your room three nights a week.
{coach} invites you onto the team's leadership council, the players who set the rules and handle the problems.
The head coach is fired the morning after the last game. Staff jobs are up in the air, and half the roster is checking the portal.

scenarios.title: The Fundraiser Nobody Wants to Run

authoring.premise: A children's hospital asks the team to run a kick-a-thon fundraiser. Someone has to organize it.
Teammates are going to the beach for spring break. Offseason lifts are optional that week, and so, it seems, are the rules.
A private kicking coach who's sent players to the pros offers you a spot in his elite group, if you drop your school's summer program.
The new head coach, Marcus Reyes, starts with a team meeting and a new rulebook. He says he's heard about every player on the roster already.
It happens again. This time it isn't only the coaches who know: a reporter is asking questions, and the team has to respond.
authoring.note: Opens only on a strike AFTER the first warning: The Coach's Office clears every strike flag, so an old strike can't open it.

authoring.premise: A man who says he works 'with' an agent finds you after practice with cash, a new phone and a promise of more.
The team votes for captains, and your name is on the ballot.
A teammate breaks team rules and asks you, as captain, to keep it in the locker room.
A pro team sends a questionnaire. Question 14: 'Describe any off-field incidents in your college career.'
An agent invites you to a steakhouse to 'talk about your future.' It's a year too early, and you both know the rules.
A kicker with a big resume transfers in from another school, and the coaches love his leg.
You've got a reputation now, and the staff is watching. {coach} offers one path back: early workouts, community hours, and no more excuses.
You're exhausted in a way sleep doesn't fix. The team counselor says taking a day isn't weakness.
The groin strain is back, worse this time, right before the conference schedule.
Someone from your old high school team calls: they're visiting campus next weekend and need a place to stay and a tour.
{sibling} got suspended from school for a fight. {parent} is overwhelmed and asks you to talk to him.
A late-night call: {parent} is in the hospital. They think it's his heart, and you're four hundred miles away with a game Saturday.
Your professor reports a possible academic integrity violation. The hearing is next week.
You have to declare a major. One keeps you eligible with the least effort; another is the one you actually care about.
A third incident. {coach} and the head coach sit you down together: one more and you're off the team. This is the last conversation before that one.
authoring.note: Opens on second_chance_used (set by the good choice in The Second Strike or The Pattern) plus a new strike. The good choice sets last_chance (no label, heavy cost); the bad one sets character_concerns. Either way, The Long Way Back stays open to anyone with the label.

authoring.premise: A teammate turns twenty-one on a Thursday and everyone is going out. Practice is at seven the next morning.
A teammate posts a video of you at a party, edited to look worse than it was. It's everywhere by morning.
A regional company offers a real NIL deal, but you'd have to promote a product you'd never use.
Your NIL money came with a tax bill nobody warned you about, and it's due next month.
{love_interest} wants you to spend the summer at home instead of at training camp. 'For once,' they say.
The person you're dating wants you to meet their family over a holiday weekend, the same weekend as the team's leadership retreat.
You and {tyler} are both finalists for the same national kicking award, and the media wants a feud.
You make a preseason watch list for the top kicker in the country. Your phone won't stop.
Your team is in the conference title race, and the campus is out of its mind. Everyone wants a piece of the players this week.
It's {holder}'s last home game, and they ask you to walk out with their family on senior day.
The pro kicker who trained you gets cut, and he calls you before he calls anyone else.
{coach} asks you to host a high school kicker on an official visit. The recruit wants to see 'the real college experience.'
Your closest friend on the team enters the transfer portal without telling you first.
After curfew, a teammate who's in no shape to drive wants to take everyone for food.
{teacher} says you're close to academic all-conference, if you take one more hard class instead of an easy elective.
The new strength coach wants you to add power fast. Your legs are already sore, and his program doesn't do rest days.
The team's leaders spend a weekend at a lake planning next season. It's also your only free weekend of the summer.
The first practice of your last college season. Everyone keeps saying it goes fast.
Pro scouts are interviewing everyone with a chance at the draft, and they've talked to people you haven't spoken to in years.
authoring.note: Open to every senior; a locked choice for rebuilt_reputation ('the long way back') joins the high school callbacks.

authoring.premise: A scout sits across from you with a folder: everything that happened in college, in writing. 'Walk me through it,' he says.
Three agents want to represent you: a big firm, a former player, and a smooth talker promising a first-round grade.
A training facility offers to prepare you for the combine. Their 'recovery program' includes things you've never heard of.
Your school's pro day is Thursday. The team's seniors are throwing a send-off party Wednesday night.
Draft weekend is coming. Do you watch with family, with teammates, or with your phone off?
You're two classes from a degree. Dropping them would free up hours for draft training.
Senior night, and your family is driving in. Before kickoff, the seniors walk out one at a time.
One last rivalry week. The younger players look to the seniors to set the tone.
{coach} asks you to speak to the team before the final game of your career.
A homesick freshman kicker reminds you of yourself four years ago.
{holder} asks you for a recommendation for a graduate assistant job. It means writing honestly about someone you love working with.
You're sore, and {coach} wants to give {backup} the kickoffs this week. {backup} looks at you before saying yes.
{tyler} is entering the draft too, and his agent suggests you two train together for the combine.
{love_interest} asks the question you've both avoided: what happens to us after college?
{parent} has driven to every game this season. You know he can't afford it.
{sibling} is a high school senior now, and college coaches are calling. He asks you how to handle them.
Draft season, final exams and your last season at once. You're short with everyone and you don't sleep.
Your knee buckles on a routine practice kick three weeks before scouts arrive.
Your last finals land in the same week as your last regular-season game.
Teammates book a senior trip in the middle of draft prep. It's the last time you'll all be together.
A national brand wants an exclusive NIL deal for your senior year. It pays more than everything else combined, and it ends all your local deals.
Your hometown asks if you'd run a free kicking camp for kids this summer. It would cost you a week and some of your NIL money.
Your class is the senior class now. The freshman initiation is your call this year.
A scout takes you to dinner and spends more time watching how you treat the waiter than asking about kicking.
Someone digs up your freshman-year posts during draft season and they're spreading.
You win an all-conference award. You have one minute at the podium.
{coach} is writing to pro scouts about you and asks what you want included, and what you'd rather leave out.
The last practice of your college career. The field is the same one you walked onto four years ago.
Your roommate admits he hasn't left the room in days and asks you not to tell anyone.
Every Sunday night the dorm goes quiet and you miss home most.
A screenshot from the team group chat leaks, and a joke you laughed at is in it.
Seven unpaid parking tickets and a hold on your registration.
A professor says, in front of the class, that athletes don't belong in her seminar.
An argument on the team bus is turning personal, and two teammates are about to swing.

scenarios.title: The Fan Who Goes Too Far

authoring.premise: A fan's messages have gone from friendly to strange. Now he says he knows where you live.
Teammates want you in a pickup basketball game. One rolled ankle could cost you a month.
A group of non-team friends parties every night, and they've started inviting you along.
A teammate wants to borrow your car for the night and won't say where he's going.
Parents offer you cash to run private kicking lessons for their kids this summer. Compliance has rules about that.
The financial aid office deposits twice what you're owed.
Team travel lands on a paper deadline. A teammate says the trick is to claim a family emergency.
Your high school coach visits campus and wants to watch you practice.
The team visits a children's hospital. Some players are there for the cameras; one kid asks you to stay longer.
Friends invite you away for a weekend off, your first in months.
The last week of your college career. Whatever happens on draft day, this is where the kicker you became walks off the field.
authoring.note: Locked choices: ready_for_pros needs combine_ready or pro_day_ready; life_after_football needs finished_degree_track; a rebuilt_reputation lock adds 'the long way back'; still_proving_it is open.
